summary: A status report documenting the assigned values from several series of numbers, including link, socket, port and protocol numbers used in network protocol implementations. It replaces RFC 990, is historic, and was replaced by RFC 1060.

eli5.summary: Computers need to agree that certain numbers mean certain things, like a phone book for protocols. This is one edition of that phone book.

questions: where were port and protocol numbers listed in 1987
what port numbers are assigned in rfc 1010
what protocol numbers does the internet use
subtitle: The official registry of Internet protocol numbers, ports, and addresses.

tldr.problem: The Internet needed a centralized way to assign and track unique numbers for protocols, ports, addresses, and other network identifiers to prevent conflicts.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents the assigned values for version numbers, protocol numbers, port numbers, domain system parameters, and other identifiers used across Internet implementations.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1010 became the canonical reference for Internet number assignments until it was superseded by RFC 1060. It served as the IANA-style registry before IANA formalized the role.

today: RFC 1010 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 1060. Today, IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) maintains the official registries of protocol numbers, port numbers, and other Internet parameters through online databases rather than published RFCs.

sections.title: Introduction and Status
sections.content:
RFC 1010 is a status report on numbers assigned in Internet protocols. It documents the current assignments from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations, including version numbers, protocol identifiers, port numbers, and other key network constants. The RFC is intended to be updated periodically and references Joyce Reynolds as the point of contact for new assignments.

The document notes that most protocols documented here are detailed in RFC notes, though some items listed are undocumented. It emphasizes that Internet protocols conventionally express numbers in decimal and use "big-endian" order for data representation, where the most significant byte appears first.
sections.eli5: This is a directory of all the numbers that computers use to talk to each other on the Internet. It explains which numbers mean what, and who to ask if you need a new one.

sections.title: Version Numbers and Protocol Identifiers
sections.content:
The RFC documents Internet Protocol version numbers, a 4-bit field identifying the protocol version. Version 4 is assigned to the Internet Protocol (IP), while other versions are reserved or unassigned. Additionally, the document lists Internet protocol numbers, an 8-bit field in the IP header identifying the next level protocol. Protocol 6 is TCP, protocol 17 is UDP, protocol 1 is ICMP, and many others are documented for use in Internet implementations.

These assignments ensure that different protocol layers can unambiguously identify each other when transmitting and receiving data over IP networks.
sections.eli5: Computers mark packets with numbers to say what kind of information is inside: is it a regular message (TCP), a quick postcard (UDP), or a status check (ICMP)? The RFC lists what each number means.

sections.title: Port Numbers and Service Assignments
sections.content:
Port numbers identify specific services on a host in TCP and UDP. The RFC assigns well-known ports to standard services: port 21 for FTP (File Transfer Protocol), port 23 for Telnet, port 25 for SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), port 53 for Domain Name Server, and many others. The assigned ports are designed so that the low-order eight bits are specified, allowing consistent assignments across TCP and UDP where possible.

The document defines reserved ports (0), unassigned ranges, and assigns specific numeric identifiers to user-facing services. This enables a client to contact a server at a predictable port number when requesting a service.
sections.eli5: A port is like a numbered mailbox on a computer. Port 21 is where file transfers arrive, port 25 is for email, port 53 is for looking up addresses. The RFC says what each number is for.

sections.title: Network-Specific Assignments and Machine Names
sections.content:
Beyond universal Internet numbers, RFC 1010 documents network-specific assignments such as ARPANET logical addresses (49,152 possible addresses with 256 reserved for well-known functions) and ARPANET link numbers, which identify message routing paths in the original ARPANET Host/IMP interface.

The RFC also includes extensive lists of official machine names and system names recognized by the Network Information Center. Machine names identify specific computer types (e.g., DEC-PDP-11, IBM-370), while system names identify operating systems (e.g., UNIX, VMS, MVS). These registries enabled network tools to recognize and categorize machines across the early Internet.
sections.eli5: Different networks and computers also got their own codes in this registry. The RFC lists the official names for computer types (like PDP-11 or IBM-370) and operating systems (like UNIX or VMS) so everyone could talk about the same machines.

sections.title: Protocol Parameters and Specialized Registries
sections.content:
RFC 1010 documents specialized number assignments for specific protocols. The Domain Name System (DNS) class parameter distinguishes address classes (Internet, Chaos), with values documented in RFC 883. IEEE 802 SAP (Service Access Point) numbers enable link-layer protocol identification on local networks, mapping between IEEE binary notation and Internet decimal notation.

The document also lists Ethernet type codes for data link layer protocol identification (2048 for IP, 2054 for ARP), Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) hardware types for different network media, and Telnet protocol option numbers for negotiating terminal features. These assignments ensure that protocols operating at different network layers can coexist and be correctly identified.
sections.eli5: Different parts of the network need their own numbering systems. Ethernet has type codes, Telnet has option numbers, and domain names have classes. The RFC keeps all these lists in one place.
